# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I've read it closely and checked the arithmetic. The tables are internally consistent: sector totals sum correctly, the employee-weighted index comes to 98.7, and each per-hour figure is the output index divided by 0.8.

The problem is with what the numbers are taken to show. The report has good raw material, but its headline conclusions go well beyond it. The most serious problems are in the reasoning, not the data.

## The central problem: "gains in every sector" is guaranteed by the method

Output per scheduled hour is defined as the output index divided by 0.8. On that definition, **any sector whose output fell by less than 20% registers a productivity "gain."** Retail could lose 15% of its output and still show +6% per hour. So "every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour" is close to automatic. It isn't a finding, and it can't support "sector-general."

The informative number is the output index itself, compared with what the deal promised: "100% of the output."
- Most sectors are near 100.
- **Retail and hospitality is at 93.1.** Output fell about 7% while pay was unchanged, so unit labour cost rose about 7.4%. By the pilot's own principle, retail did not meet the deal.

Calling this "output per hour rose 16.4%... notable" turns the weakest result into a selling point.

## The report's own data contradicts "sector-general"

Look at who reverted:

| | Organisations | Reverted | Reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | **50%** |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 2 | **40%** |
| All other sectors | 50 | 0 | **0%** |

All five reversions came from the two sectors with the lowest output. Half of the retail organisations abandoned the schedule. These are the same sectors where coverage constraints were expected to bite.

The fair reading of the data is the opposite of the conclusion. The model held up in office and knowledge work and struggled where output is tied to time on the floor. The headline "92% continued" hides this split.

## Other problems, roughly by importance

**1. The output measure is the weakest link, and it's dismissed too quickly.**
- The primary outcome is a manager's judgement.
- Each manager used whatever records their organisation held, with no common definition.
- Those managers were responsible for the pilot's success.

An index clustered just under 100 is exactly what you'd expect from people asked "roughly unchanged?" about a scheme they championed and their staff value. The limitations section says these issues are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency." But the size comes from dividing by 0.8, and the consistency comes from the shared measure. Neither can count as evidence against the measure's bias.

**2. Scheduled hours are not hours worked.**
Limitation 4 concedes this but doesn't connect it to the per-hour figures. Two things point toward actual hours falling by less than 20%:
- Some staff worked on their day off or lengthened their remaining days.
- 17 organisations staggered days off "to maintain coverage."

The +23.4% therefore overstates productivity by an unknown amount. If actual hours fell by only 10%, the gain is about 10%, not 23%.

**3. The revenue figure probably shows a real decline.**
The pilot ran in 2023. A nominal increase of 1.4% year on year, against inflation of several percent across most economies at that time, means real revenue fell. On top of that:
- 9 of 61 organisations didn't report revenue.
- Revenue is employee-weighted, which is an unusual choice.

"Offers no sign that output was sacrificed" doesn't follow. Adjusted for inflation, it may offer exactly that sign.

**4. Sick days and resignations aren't adjusted for season.**
Revenue was compared with the same months a year earlier "to remove seasonality." Sick days and resignations, however, were compared with the *six months immediately before*. If the baseline included winter and the pilot ran through spring and summer, a large fall in sick days is expected anyway.

Resignations also fell across labour markets during 2023 as post-pandemic turnover cooled. And a four-day week at full pay is a perk that is costly to leave, whatever happens to fatigue.

**5. Attrition and survivorship.**
Seventy organisations enrolled and nine withdrew "chiefly for scheduling reasons." Those are plausibly the cases where coverage made the scheme hardest, so excluding them flatters the results. We need to know which sectors the nine came from. The varying denominators (61, 58 interviews, 52 revenue reports) should also be stated in the summary.

**6. The wellbeing data shows fading, which the report doesn't discuss.**
Energy rose by 0.61 SD at month three, then fell back to 0.29 SD by month six, so more than half the gain faded within three months. That is the pattern of a novelty or Hawthorne effect. It bears directly on limitation 5 ("longer-run effects in either direction"), and the data already hints at the direction. Similarly, "64% rated their productivity higher" is self-report from people with a strong interest in the scheme continuing.

**7. The fatigue explanation is asserted, not tested.**
Nothing in the design separates two explanations:
- reduced fatigue,
- process changes: fewer meetings, focus blocks, simpler approvals.

Managers' own accounts point to process changes. 47 of 58 mentioned meetings, and several called the schedule "a forcing device" for changes they'd long wanted. If process changes drove the result, much of it could be had *without* cutting hours. That is a very different policy conclusion.

**8. Continuation isn't independent evidence.**
The same self-selected organisations decided whether to continue. Removing a popular benefit is costly in morale and retention, whatever its effect on productivity. Only 18 made it permanent, so the other 38 may still be provisional. And continuation was decidedly not universal in the sectors where it matters most.

**9. No variation is reported.**
There are no confidence intervals, no spread across organisations, and no monthly trajectory, even though the index was collected monthly. Some sectors contain only 5 or 6 organisations, where one outlier could move the mean.

## What the evidence does support

The pilot is still useful. A defensible summary would say something like:

> In 61 self-selected organisations, mostly in office-based sectors, managers reported output close to baseline after scheduled hours were cut by 20%. Sickness absence, resignations and reported burnout fell, though some measures were not seasonally adjusted and self-reported energy declined between months three and six. Results were weaker in retail/hospitality and healthcare administration, where output fell 3–7% and 5 of 11 organisations reverted. Without a control group, measured working hours, or an independent output measure, the size of any productivity gain is uncertain, and the findings do not establish that the model generalises across sectors.

## Suggested changes to the paper

1. Drop "sector-general" from the summary and conclusion. Report reversion by sector in the main results.
2. Lead with the output index. Present per-hour figures only alongside actual-hours data, or with explicit caveats.
3. Report revenue in real terms.
4. Seasonally adjust sick days and resignations, or compare them with the same months of the prior year.
5. Report which sectors the nine withdrawn organisations came from.
6. Add the monthly output trajectory, spread across organisations, and confidence intervals.
7. Replace "unlikely to overturn the main result" with an honest assessment of how each limitation could bias the estimate, and in which direction.
8. Put "further pilots include a comparison group" up front as a priority. At present the recommendation sits uneasily beside a very confident conclusion.

I can redraft the Summary and Discussion along these lines if that would help, or rebuild Table 1 with sector reversion rates and unit labour cost added.
